unit.title: Numbers and Sequences
unit.blurb: Counting on and back in steps, linear sequences and their rules, square and cube numbers, prime numbers, and common multiples and factors.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Count on and back in steps of constant size, including decimals and negative numbers, and continue sequences.

O2.t: Recognise square numbers, cube numbers and prime numbers.

O3.t: Find common multiples and common factors of two numbers.

p: A **sequence** is a list of numbers that follow a rule. 3, 7, 11, 15, … starts at 3 and the **term-to-term rule** is 'add 4'.
You can count in decimals (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, …) and below zero (5, 2, −1, −4, …).
The **position-to-term rule** links a term to its position: for 3, 6, 9, 12, … the term is 3 × the position, so the 10th term is 30.

lesson.t: Why the term-to-term rule is not enough for far terms
p: Adding the step again and again works, but for the 100th term it is slow. A rule linked to the position lets us jump straight there.

lesson.q: A sequence is 3, 6, 9, 12, … What is the 20th term?

p: A **square number** is a number times itself: 6 × 6 = 6² = 36. A **cube number** is a number used three times: 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8.
A **prime number** has exactly two factors, 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, … 1 is not prime.

lesson.t: Why square numbers are called square
p: 16 counters can be arranged in a 4 by 4 square: 16 = 4 × 4 = 4². That is why we say '4 squared'.
A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, so its counters only make one row. 1 is not prime: it has only one factor.
Square: the number × itself.
Cube: the number × itself × itself.
Learn squares to 12 × 12 and cubes to 5 × 5 × 5.
2 is the only even prime number.

options.fb: Correct.

p: **Multiples** of 4 are in the 4 times table: 4, 8, 12, 16, … A **common multiple** of 4 and 6 is in both lists: 12, 24, …
**Factors** of 12 divide into 12 exactly: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. A **common factor** of 12 and 18 divides into both: 1, 2, 3, 6.
